title: September deliberations weigh new US tariffs against persistent fuel costs at 2.25%
summary: In the deliberations published on 16 September, Governing Council explained why it maintained the overnight rate at 2.25% on 2 September even though both sets of risks surrounding the July outlook had worsened. New US tariffs and the breakdown in trade talks threatened a recovery that had finally broadened. Curtailed shipping and refinery damage were also keeping petrol and diesel expensive for longer. The policy question was whether the resulting weakness in demand would constrain firms’ ability to pass rising costs on, or whether persistent energy inflation would ultimately reach a wider set of prices. A count of adverse headlines by itself cannot resolve the direction of the next rate move (Considerations for monetary policy and Policy decision).

GDP rebounded 3.3% in the second quarter, exceeding expectations slightly after two weak quarters. Temporary factors magnified the number, but consumer spending, exports, business investment and housing all showed improvement. The condominium markets in Toronto and Vancouver remained soft. Private-sector job creation was solid, yet unemployment was still around 6½% and wages grew moderately. Members agreed that the economy remained in excess supply and differed on how much slack remained. A short period of above-potential growth can narrow an existing output gap without eliminating it. The economy had therefore entered the new tariff episode on a stronger footing than earlier in the year while remaining vulnerable to a fall in investment or hiring (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The newly imposed US tariffs covered roughly 5% of Canadian goods exports to the United States. That denominator matters: it was neither 5% of Canadian GDP nor 5% of total international trade. The direct aggregate effect was expected to be modest, but affected businesses and workers could experience large losses. Fiscal measures and firms’ adaptations could offset some effects. Meanwhile, diminished confidence and the threat of escalation could delay hiring and investment in sectors not yet directly covered. Canada’s counter-tariffs mostly affected intermediate inputs or goods for which Canadian substitutes existed. Members judged the immediate CPI impact would be muted and spread through time. The export-demand and domestic input-price channels therefore had different exposures and lags (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Considerations for monetary policy).

Headline CPI had hovered near 3% for several months. Excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2% and the core measures remained near 2%. With the Strait of Hormuz restricted, expectations for crude prices had risen. Damage to Middle Eastern and Russian refining capacity and planned maintenance kept refinery margins unusually high. Those margins determine how much a movement in crude changes the price of petrol at the pump. Even with little observed pass-through into other components, an extended period of higher diesel and petrol prices would increase the probability of costs spreading over time. Members distinguished that growing risk from an established broad inflation process at the time of the meeting (International economy and Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The July baseline had assumed existing US tariffs remained, the North American trade agreement continued with annual reviews, and shipping gradually normalised, lowering oil prices. Subsequent Canadian activity and consumer prices had been broadly consistent with the projection to date, but assumptions underpinning its future path were less secure. Renewed trade uncertainty could make the recovery less durable. Higher oil and refining costs could hold headline inflation farther from the target for longer. International bond yields had risen with sovereign-debt concerns and expectations that central banks would tighten against inflation. Canadian yields rose by less than in several peers, and the Canadian dollar appreciated slightly as the US dollar weakened. Those moves offer alternatives to a purely Canadian policy explanation for changes in discount rates and imported prices (International economy and Considerations for monetary policy).

Members’ different assessments of slack and the impact of tariffs mattered because they implied different strengths of pricing power. A firm experiencing a sudden loss of customers may accept a margin squeeze when its fuel bill rises. A firm able to preserve sales at a higher price can pass the cost on. A prolonged shock could expose both groups to repeated cost increases even where the initial CPI effect was narrow. Council judged it needed to observe whether recovery survived the new tariffs and whether non-energy prices began to respond. This judgement carried no published vote count, numerical trigger for tightening or presumption that broader inflation would follow automatically from time spent above target (Considerations for monetary policy).

For policy, the common reference point remained the forecast for inflation. Slower growth would enter that forecast by increasing spare capacity and reducing pass-through. More persistent energy costs would enter through both the direct CPI contribution and their potential effects on other prices. The fact that growth and inflation posed opposing risks did not establish that their magnitudes cancelled. It established a reason to retain 2.25% on the available evidence and to revise the judgement if the distribution of outcomes shifted. In an event study, the 2 September announcement and the 16 September publication should be measured separately, with the tariff and global rates news between them preserved as separate events (Policy decision).

questions.question: How much of the response to the new US tariffs occurred outside the directly affected export lines?
questions.detail: Compare shipments, orders, hiring and investment in the products covered by tariffs against similar products and domestic industries. Track how reported uncertainty shifts before any tariffs extend to additional products. Keep exposure relative to US-bound goods exports distinct from exposure relative to total sales, and account for fiscal support. Direct losses and the option value of delaying investment are separate mechanisms.

questions.question: Did wider refinery margins explain persistent headline inflation without broader repricing?
questions.detail: Decompose Canadian fuel prices into crude costs, currency, refining and distribution margins. Measure subsequent changes in component-level CPI and the prices of transport-intensive goods. If non-energy prices stay subdued as domestic fuel prices remain elevated, the direct contribution remains the stronger explanation. Persistent changes in prices or wages of unrelated sectors would require a different account.

questions.question: Was rising GDP evidence of a smaller output gap than Council had assumed?
questions.detail: Estimate how much of second-quarter growth reflected temporary contributions and compare persistent orders, hours, job finding, wages and capacity use across sectors. Track fiscal measures and trade exposure separately. A rebound from two weak quarters can coexist with continuing slack. Evidence of stronger pricing power at firms with newly rising orders would more directly connect the growth surprise to future inflation.
